Precious Metals Quarterly 2010 Q1 

# Executive summary 

## Palladium: a tighter market 

The palladium market should normalise from 2010, after its 2009 dislocation.  We expect smaller fundamental surpluses from 2011 and much less pronounced Russian official stockpile sales.  High marginal PGM production costs, a tightening physical market and investmentrelated demand for hard assets should support the price.  We now see room for prices to be approaching $500/oz in real terms by the end of our forecast period.  And there may be further upside potential if the growth of petrol vehicles fitted with emissions after-treatment systems proves stronger than we expect and/or there is more rapid substitution of palladium for platinum and even rhodium in automotive after-treatment applications.  Even without this, we expect the platinum:palladium price ratio to fall towards the levels of the early 2000s over our forecast period. 

After bouncing this year, the delayed response of jewellery manufacturers to already higher prices could dampen total consumption growth in 2011.  But 2012 should then see the start of a longer-lasting upturn even if palladium continues to under-perform in Western markets.  We expect the automotive sector to remain the major source of palladium demand.  And there will be very strong production growth of light duty petrol fuelled vehicles fitted with palladium rich autocatalyst devices in developing economies.  Palladium loadings on diesel (and petrol) emissions after-treatment systems will also rise as higher quality fuels become more widely available.  Developing populous economies such as India and China will therefore account for an increasing proportion of global offtake. 

Delayed investment means miners will struggle to meet this increase in industrial consumption.  Higher PGM prices into 2010 have led to less challenging capital financing conditions for PGM producers.  But increased regulatory focus since the start of the year on reducing trading liquidity in financial and commodity markets and raising banks’ capital reserves suggest producers’ ability to access external funding may be constrained for longer than we had previously thought – to now beyond 2010.  So producers will continue to prioritise cost management and optimisation of existing mining operations, and capital expenditure plans will remain subject to review.  Meanwhile, in South Africa, we do not expect platinum prices to comfortably exceed the estimated marginal cost of production on a sustained basis over our forecast period, and this will hold back associated by-product palladium supply.  And uncertainty regarding the application of Zimbabwe’s BEE legislation will make companies more cautious about investing there, although it is not clear the extent to which these investments will be directed to other regions.

## Other precious metal markets 

### Go

ld 

We still take the view that re-monetisation of gold, at the national and international level, will be a dominant driver of the gold price, despite the recent change in market psychology favouring the US dollar. 



- Taking account of the pull-back in the gold price from over $1,200/oz in early December 2009, we have lowered our 2010 Q1-Q3 forecasts, but have kept our 2011-14 price outlook unchanged for the time being.  We still expect nominal gold prices to remain mostly above $1,100/oz. 



- Whether or not gold is included in any recomposed IMF SDR basket in late 2010 (it could be deferred to the next review in 2015) will set the scene for what subsequently happens to the gold price. 



- The sharp rise in bullion prices and producer margins has led to an increase in actual and potential mine supply, but longer-term gold mine supply remains constrained. 

### Silver 

Our latest tabulations confirm that the market’s surplus swelled to the equivalent of 20% of fabrication demand in 2009.  Even with offtake recovering strongly through to 2014, production restraint is needed if a more balanced market is to develop.  And this needs lower prices. 



- Mine production is estimated to have increased by 1,050 tonnes in 2009, and further growth could result in market surpluses of a similar magnitude continuing through to 2014 if silver’s price does not fall towards $8/oz before then. 



- Even outside China, economic recovery is now lifting fabrication demand. 

### Platinum 

We still expect the platinum market to return to a period of sustained deficits from 2011. 



- This tightening of the physical market combined with high marginal production costs and continued investment-related demand for hard assets should support the price.  We have raised our forecasts to average around $1,490/oz in real terms over 2010-14. 



- Institutional and high net worth individuals could have a far greater influence on price and metal availability than in the past.  But we still expect liquidation of platinum ETF holdings to be stickier than that of previously held asset classes. 



- Northam Platinum has begun an early works programme to construct roads, pipelines and infrastructure facilities for its greenfield Booysendal mine, with Phase 1 construction goahead likely in July 2010 and first production in 2011.  Meanwhile, Eastern Platinum has restarted the development of the Crocette Section of its Crocodile River plant, which had been put on hold in December 2008.

## Data sources and study team 

The historical data presented in this report are based on estimates published by a variety of sources, including Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), CPM, GTIS trade statistics, company websites and written reports. 

However, CRU’s interpretation of the data may or may not coincide with those expressed in these various sources. 

The forecast is exclusively CRU’s.
